data.text:
Enterprise clients are a different beast.
It almost cost me $5.2M to learn these lessons:

We had just closed the biggest deal in GrowthAssistant's history.

50+ Growth Assistants. Beautiful structure. I was excited.

And then... problems.
Tracking, metrics, task completion, and comms breakdown.

"Overall, this has been disappointing.

We are considering terminating the whole deal."

My heart sank. This client churning would set the business back a year.

I flew out to Boston with my top team, and we dug in.

I created a special ops force, went into the client's systems, and spent 4 weeks with them and the GAs to get things back on track.

At the end, we navigated it.

Here's what you need to know about servicing enterprise clients:

1. Right Clients Matter
Not all big logos are good clients. Some lack processes, internal alignment, or readiness to integrate new solutions.

2. Align on Success Metrics and Keep Talking About Them
Regular check-ins, reporting, and aligning on performance expectations prevent misalignment.

3. Proactive Problem-Solving Wins Trust
Don't wait for your clients to point out issues. Build the dashboards early. If you predict a problem and provide solutions, it sets you apart.

4. Visibility and Resources
More stakeholder involvement, visibility into their systems, and careful resource planning to handle fluctuating demands.

5. Involve Leadership
For our biggest clients, I get involved in the weeds and talk to POCs. Before you have the playbooks, you need to give it your best shot.

I could pull this off because of the team around me.

Our US team of 20 is supported by 50+ Growth Assistants in the Philippines.

They take care of execution and day-to-day. So we can focus on strategy and problem-solving.

DoorDash, Calm, HubSpot, and 200 others use us to hire elite global talent for their teams. 

Start growing lean: https://t.co/OmoS1Z2YvW

Volt Bohol was in grade school when former Sen. Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino, Jr., was shot dead upon his arrival at the Manila International Airport that for almost 40 years now bears his name.

By Bohol’s admission, he must not have been “at the right age” to look inside the coffin of the fallen opposition leader, whose bloodied body laid in state at the Santo Domingo Church just beside his school.

Now, 53, Bohol is the president of the organization put up by Ninoy’s brother, Agapito or Butz, to rally mainstream protest against the assassination of the senator, as well as against the country’s ills, which remained decades after the EDSA Revolution in 1986.
